Before we get into today's agenda, I'd like to take a moment to acknowledge two dates
of significance.
The first is the International Day for the Elimination of Racial Discrimination, which
will be this Friday, March 21, 2025.
On Friday, Kitchener will join communities around the world in marking the International
Day for the Elimination of Racial Discrimination.
As a community, we stand in solidarity with cities around the globe in our commitment
to eradicate all forms of racism.
This day serves as a powerful reminder of our shared commitment to combat all forms
of racism within our community and beyond. As a city that celebrates and takes pride
in its vibrant and diverse culture with almost one-third of our residents identifying as
Indigenous, Black or racialized, we recognize the importance of fostering an inclusive environment
where every individual is treated with dignity and respect, free from our community, continue
to face discrimination and work together to eliminate it. As a community, we have an
abundance of opportunities to learn, share and connect with each other as well as we
affirm our collective responsibility to challenge and confront racism wherever it exists.
Racial discrimination violates the fundamental principles of equality and human rights and
undermines the fabric of our communities. It perpetuates division, inequality and injustice,
hindering the progress and prosperity of nations around the world. It is essential that we
continue to foster an inclusive and equitable city that values and welcomes everyone.
In recent years, the City of Kitchener has significantly expanded its efforts to combat
racial discrimination through collaborations with community partners and a focus on education
and resource development for both City Council and staff.
In 2022, we launched the Racialized and Indigenous Supports for Equity or RISE fund to support
Black, Indigenous and other racialized community-led programs and initiatives.
Since its launch, the RISE fund has awarded $396,789 in grants to Black, Indigenous and other
racialized community-led programs, projects and events. Through its SDG Idea Factory,
the City has invested in supporting underrepresented groups and equity-deserving entrepreneurs.
This initiative offers resources such as innovative space, business coaching and workshops
to help entrepreneurs contribute to the achievement of all 17 UN Sustainable Development Goals,
particularly Goal 10, Reducing Inequalities, and Goal 17, Partnerships for the Goals.
Together, as a Council and as staff, we remain committed to building a city that is not only
diverse but also inclusive, equitable, and free from discrimination.
Together, let's strive to build a world where every individual is treated with dignity,
respect and equity regardless of race or ethnicity. Today and every day,
let's join our Kitchener community as we stand against racial discrimination.
Colleagues, I'd also like to acknowledge that beginning on March 11th and through to March 25th,
we've been marking the five-year anniversary since the declaration of COVID-19 as a global pandemic.
March 11, as you know, is the global day in memory of those lost during COVID-19.
Today is five years since the provincial emergency was declared, and March 25 will mark five years
since the City of Kitchener joined local municipalities in declaring a state of emergency
due to the COVID-19 global pandemic. The state of emergency provided flexibility at the time for the
city to respond quickly to the pandemic and that state of emergency ended two years later.
I think as we all reflect back on those days, we'll recognize that in particular those first
two years were tough. The story of our community was in a way one that saw its share of sorrow and
fear. Residents lost loved ones, in some cases lost their livelihoods and lost important connections
to friends, family and colleagues. We missed important milestones, stayed apart and made
public health measures part of our everyday lives. Over those initial two years in particular,
we saw some of the best that our community's human spirit was capable of. As we moved forward,
we recognized that we had a shared resilience and a renewed sense of hope and optimism ensued
as we came out of the pandemic. It's something that collectively we've all worked on over the
last three years even though beyond those initial two years COVID-19 still is something that exists
in our communities and impacts residents but we obviously have resources in place including the
vaccine that have helped ensure people can navigate through it in a way that doesn't
impact their lives in the same way. But throughout this whole time and
particularly in those initial two years, many essential service workers, first
responders, health care heroes and community volunteers helped all of us
through COVID-19 with unwavering dignity and grace. And so on behalf of this
Council, I want to take this opportunity to once again thank everyone who was
part of the community's COVID-19 response. I think as we reflected this
morning, as we consider our community's response to a different kind of challenge,
namely the challenge of an economic tariff war with the United States, that
too is bringing its own challenges to the community and once again requiring
us all to come together as a community and support each other as we navigate through the challenges
in the road before us. But what COVID taught us is that when we weather these challenges with hope,
with humour and creativity, we in fact as a community can demonstrate the resilience that's
necessary to be to demonstrate care and compassion to each other and to demonstrate that in fact we
can be heroes for each other as we look through these challenges. So as we mark this fifth year
anniversary, we want to reflect both on those who have been impacted, which is all of us,
by COVID-19, but in particular those in our community, in our family and friend circles,
who lost their lives to COVID-19. And at this point, I'd like to invite everyone to stand for
a moment of silence as we remember those who lost their lives during COVID.

Good afternoon, members of Council.
On behalf of Task Force Chair Vrbanovic and members of Kitchener's Tariff and Trade Task
Force, I'm pleased to provide an update on the work of the Task Force today.
Today marks day 14 of heightened, deliberate and unprovoked economic tension between the
United States and Canada.
Over these past two weeks and indeed over the past two months preceding them, an incredible
amount of economic uncertainty and even angst has been created, the likes of which we have
not experienced as a country in recent history.
As a response to this uncertainty, on February 10th, you unanimously adopted a resolution
to initiate a response to these new economic realities.
Based on the urgency of your resolution, a City of Kitchener Tariff and Trade Task Force
was immediately assembled to facilitate timely action.
I'm pleased to report that over the last four weeks, our task force has come together
with a clear purpose, with a sense of urgency and a strong resolve to ensure that Kitchener's
interests, and by extension Canada's interests, are protected now and in the coming days.
Co-chaired by Mayor Vrbanovic and myself, our task force has worked collaboratively
in consultation with community partners, with businesses and with internal subject matter
experts to understand the tariff vulnerability of economic sectors within the City of Kitchener.
We've also heeded national, provincial and territorial calls for municipalities to step
up and support Canadian efforts in weathering this economic crisis with the United Front.
Together, our work has been grounded in the principles that you'll note on the screen,
which have informed the ultimate direction of our work.
I'm happy to now provide a high-level overview of the initial action plan.
Our first proposed action is to amend Kitchener's procurement by-law, which will be brought
forward for your consideration in the next committee cycle.
Municipalities across Canada are required to comply with a range of trade agreements
which set minimum dollar thresholds for competitive procurement and therefore limit municipalities
from exclusively buying Canadian.
For purchases that fall below these thresholds, there is more flexibility to conduct targeted
activities that prioritize Canadian purchases.
Since our procurement by-law was last reviewed, the prescribed trade agreement limits have
changed, and by adjusting the limits within our own by-law, we can increase our flexibility
to prioritize Canadian procurement for higher-value purchases.
Second, thanks to the good work of our procurement team, the task force is pleased to report
that 98 per cent of the City's goods, services and construction are already sourced from
Ontario-based businesses where they are part of a formal procurement process.
This is a significant accomplishment that not only limits our overall tariff exposure,
but it also demonstrates our existing commitment to support our local and provincial economy.
But there's still work to be done to limit tariff exposure.
The City uses nearly 50 distributors that source product from the U.S. that is used
in our municipal operations.
And we're prioritizing dialogue with these distributors to highlight the importance that
we are placing on Canadian preference and to explore opportunities for import substitution.
Third, year over year, the City purchases a limited number of small-dollar supply items
that are used in municipal operations, some of which is supplied through the U.S.
By shifting away from buying product from the U.S. where possible, we can symbolically support the actions of the federal and provincial government and support our local economy.
In some cases, there may not be alternatives. However, staff will be encouraged to prioritize Canadian purchases wherever possible.

Fourth, through the work of our task force, we want to assure our residents, businesses and workers that the City is actively monitoring impacts to our local economy and engaging in meaningful conversations with tariff-impacted businesses.
A comprehensive outreach plan has been developed and is being deployed to understand the challenges
and opportunities that are facing these sectors.
In collaboration with other area municipalities and the Waterloo Economic Development Corporation,
work is underway to support local manufacturing and to create resources to support import
substitution again for local businesses.
And five, earlier this afternoon, each of you participated in the kickoff of our Support
Local campaign that will be undertaken in partnership with our BIAs in downtown Kitchener
and Belmont Village and the local Chamber of Commerce. There are several initiatives
within this program that will be rolled out in the Kitchener market in the coming weeks
as well to help support shoppers make informed decisions about supporting local.
Each of the five actions identified have been developed for immediate implementation. Work
has commenced on all of them and will be well underway by April 1.
As the current economic situation continues to unfold, Kitchener's Tariff and Trade Task
Force will be active to respond quickly to changing circumstances.
We'll continue to play our part to see Kitchener through this crisis.
Staff leadership from our task force are present this afternoon to my left and also to my right,
along with Mayor Vrbanovic and Councillor Davey who is serving on the task force.
And with that, we're all pleased to receive any questions or comments that you have about
our work to date.
